soma
------------------------------------------
The word ‘soma’ has been used in several senses. One of the common meaning is चन्द्र or the deity मोओन्. He is the presiding deity of Somavāra or Monday and one of the नवग्रहस् or Nine प्लनेत्स्. (See CANDRA for details.)
In the वेदस् it has been used to indicate the सोम-creeper, as also its juice, somarasa, which is extensively used to offer as oblations in Somayāgas. The twigs of the creeper were brown or tawny in colour and would hang down. It used to grow on hills and mountains. Hence it was difficult for ordinary people to obtain it. Probably some of the hill-tribes were experts in collecting these creepers and supplying them.
Crushing the stalks of this creeper to extract the juice was also a part of Vedic ritualism. This was called ‘abhiṣava’ or ‘savana’.
The stalks were probably kept immersed in water and then crushed with the stones called grāva and adri, The juice was then filtered in दशापवित्र (made of wool) into a vessel called द्रोणकलश.
Camū was the name of the vessel containing the somarasa for gods. The vessels used by the priests for drinking it were called कलश and चमस (all made of wood).
In Somayāgas, the सवन or the extraction of the सोम juice from the creepers was done thrice a day: morning (prātassavana), noon (mādhyandina-सवन) and evening (tṛtīyasavana). The presiding deities of these were इन्द्र, Maruts and विश्वेदेवस् for the first, इन्द्र alone for the second and the ऋभुस् (human beings raised to the status of gods) for the third.
The सोम juice is sometimes mixed with milk or curds or barley. Then it is called gavāśira, daddhyāśira and yavāśira respectively.
Soma is a highly exhilarating drink that induces tremendous energy. इन्द्र is said to be very fond of it; so also the gods to whom it is offered as libation.
It is not at all an intoxicating drink like liquor though, sometimes, prejudiced and ignorant Western scholars dub it so.
Soma seems to have become a rare plant and gone out of vogue even by the time of the Vedic ब्राह्मणस्. Hence several substitutes like extracts of phālguna plants, pūtikā stalks, dūb plants and greenish कुश grass have been prescribed.

Somayāga
(‘Vedic sacrifice [using] सोम juice’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices—called yāgas and yajñas—are generally classified into three groups, out of which the Somayāgas form the last. They are called so since the सोम juice is the main ingredient of the oblations.
There are seven Somayāgas which are the models. They are: अग्निष्टोम, अप्तोर्याम, अतिरात्र, Atyagniṣṭoma, Śoḍaśī, Ukthya and वाजपेय.
A सोमयाग needs mantras from all the three Vedas—Ṛgveda, Yajurveda and Sāmaveda—as also all the sixteen ṛtviks or priests.
The सोम juice is extracted from the creeper three times. The extraction is called prātassavana, mādhyandinasavana and tṛtīyasavana, done in the morning, noon and late afternoon.
See AGNIṢṬOMA and VEDIC SACRIFICES.

Somanāthapura
------------------------------------------
Somanāthapura is a small town 40 kms. from the Mysore city, Karnataka. Somanātha, who was a minister of the king नरसिṁह (the Third) of the Hoysaḷa dynasty, is said to have built this as an agrahara (a small township for ब्राह्मणस्). He built two temples, one for विष्णु and the other for शिव in A.

. The former is known as the Keśava temple and the latter as the Pañcaliṅgeśvara temple.
सोमनाथपुर Temple">A View of the सोमनाथपुर TempleThe Keśava temple stands in the centre of the courtyard measuring 65 metres (218 ft.) by 35 metres (117 ft.). It has three sanctums and three towers, each of 9 1/2 metres (32 ft.) height. The whole structure is on a जगती (platform) almost a metre high. Attached to the high prākāra (boundary wall) there are 64 verandah-like structures with pillars.
The towers (vimāna) of the sanctum have a few beautiful sculptures. The vimānas are capped with inverted lotus-like structures.
The prākāra has three rows of figures depicting scenes form the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata.
Out of the three garbhagṛhas or sanctums, the central one is empty. It is said to have contained the image of Keśava. The other two shrines contain the images of Janārdana and Veṇugopāla (aspects of विष्णु).
Some of the beautifully carved images are those of Nṛtyagaṇapati, Nṛtyalakṣmī, इन्द्र on his royal elephant ऐरावत, Kūrmāvatāra (Tortoise इन्चर्नतिओन्), दुर्गा, सरस्वती and परशुराम.
The शिव temple has five sanctums for five aspects of शिव: Bijjaleśvara, Pergaḍeśvara, Revaleśvara, Bayiraleśvara and Somanātheśvara. Though these shrines are independent, they have a common verandah or portico.
The Keśava temple is an excellent specimen of Hoysaḷa Architecture, rivalling the ones in Belūr and हऌएबीडु.

somasūtra
------------------------------------------
Śiva is said to be fond of shower bath as also a regular bath! Hence, the Śivalliṅgas (or liṅgas) installed in temples are bathed either continuously or during the ceremonial worship. On one side of the लिङ्ग, there is a small projected channel to convey the water thus poured, to a vessel kept below it. This channel is called ‘somasūtra’. While circumambulating the लिङ्ग, the सोमसूत्र should not be crossed. The devotee should start from it, go round the लिङ्ग clockwise and return anticlockwise after reaching the other side of the same.
The water collected in the vessel is used as tīrtha (consecrated water for sipping) by the devotees.
See also ŚIVALIṄGA.

Somnāth Temple
------------------------------------------
The temple of Somnāth—also spelt as Somanātha—can rightly be described as the phoenix of the Hindu ethos. No sooner was the temple razed to the ground by the barbarian marauders who invaded the country (India) than it would rise again!
Somanāth Temple at GujaratSituated in the small town of Prabhās Paṭan in the Saurashtra area of the modern Gujarat state, on the shore of the Arabian Sea, it is the first of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् (‘liṅgas of light’) mentioned in the पुराणस्.
The original icon, called the Sparśaliṅga (almost the size of a hen’s egg), was vouchsafed to सोम (the deity मोओन्) by Lord शिव who was immensely pleased by his severe austerities. Hence, the लिङ्ग got the appellation Somanātha (Lord of सोम or the मोओन्).
The first temple over it was, as per legend, built by मोओन् in gold. Subsequently—as it was ravaged in course of time—it was rebuilt by रावण in silver, by कृष्ण in wood and by भीम in stone.
Prabhās Paṭan is an important pilgrim centre, associated with कृष्ण’s final departure from the world. The river सरस्वती was said to join the ocean here.
There is a reference to Somnāth even in the Ṛgveda (khila part at the end of the 9th मण्डल).
The Prabhāsakhaṇḍa of the Skanda-purāṇa deals with this subject in great detail.
Historically, one of the first temples might have been built by the Valabhī kings sometime during the 5th century A. D. From the ruins at the site, it is surmised that a temple might have existed even in A.

.
This place was a stronghold of the पाशुपत cult started by लकुलीश before A.

.
The सोम्नाथ् तेम्प्ले was the wealthiest at its time, before being looted by Ghazni Mohammed in A.

. The earnings from ten thousand villages were dedicated to it as offering. For the daily worship, water was being brought from the river गङ्गा and flowers from Kāśmīra. One thousand ब्राह्मणस् were engaged in its worship, in various ways. A very heavy chain of gold was used to ring the temple bell.
The temple hall (raṅgamaṇḍapa) contained 56 gem-studded pillars, each encrusted with gold sheets.
The लिङ्ग in the गर्भगृह or the sanctum was 3 metres (10 ft.) high and 1.8 metres (6 ft.) in diameter. The sanctum itself was very majestic. There were three paths leading to it.
A golden palanquin had been gifted by the Solaṅki king Bhīmdev, to carry the उत्सवमूर्ति (processional icon).
This very wealth and splendour tempted Ghazni Mohammed to plunder and destroy the temple in A.

.
Thereafter, reconstruction by the local kings and destruction by the Muslim invaders went on for several centuries, the last destruction being the one by Aurangazeb in A.

.
Ahalyabai Holkar built another temple near the ruins in A.

.
After independence, the temple was rebuilt, the गर्भगृह being located in the original place, the शिवलिङ्ग being established on the same ब्रह्मशिला (See BRAHMAŚILĀ.). The credit goes mainly to Sardār Vallabh-bhai Paṭel (A.
-1950), the then Deputy Prime Minister of India. Dr. Rājendra Prasād (A.

-1963) the then President of India, opened the rebuilt shrine on the 11th May 1951. The whole complex was completed only in 1995. Dr. Śaṅkar Dayāl Śarma, who was the President of India at that time, dedicated it on 1st December. It has been built in the Cālukyan type of temple architecture.
The विमान (tower over the sanctum) of the new temple is 50 metres (164 ft.) high. There are intricate carvings and silver doors. The नन्दि (reclining bull) is quite elegant. Other इदोल्स् also find appropriate places in the temple-complex.
In and around the सोम्नाथ् तेम्प्ले there are quite a few places of religious significance like गीता Mandir, लक्ष्मी-nārāyaṇ Temple, Baldev-gufā (cave), Triveṇīsaṅgam, Paraśurāmakṣetra, Sun-temple and others.
A statue of Sardār Paṭel stands out in the precincts, in commemoration of his historic association with the reconstruction of this temple of Somnāth.
